summary: Specifies RTP payload formats for the Enhanced Variable Rate Narrowband-Wideband speech codec, EVRC-NW, with three media type registrations. It also specifies a file format for storing the speech data, for use in places such as email.

eli5.summary: Instructions for packing voice recordings into small packages for sending over the internet, plus a way to save them in a file.

subtitle: How to carry EVRC-NW compressed speech in RTP packets, store it in files and negotiate it with SDP.

tldr.problem: The EVRC-NW speech codec needed a defined way to travel inside RTP packets, to be described in SDP and to be saved in files such as email attachments.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reuses the existing EVRC packet formats, adds one capability flag bit for wideband versus narrowband encoding, registers three media subtypes and defines a simple storage file format.
tldr.outcome: IP phones, media gateways and voice messaging servers can exchange EVRC-NW speech and negotiate it alongside EVRC-B and EVRC-WB.

today: RFC 6884 is a Proposed Standard from March 2013. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the RFC Defines
sections.content:
RFC 6884 specifies how to packetize speech encoded with the Enhanced Variable Rate Narrowband-Wideband Codec (EVRC-NW) into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP). It covers three packet formats: header-free, interleaved/bundled and compact bundle. It also covers discontinuous transmission (DTX) support.

The RFC says EVRC-NW offers better speech quality than the EVRC and EVRC-B codecs and better capacity than the Enhanced Variable Rate Wideband Codec (EVRC-WB). Besides the RTP formats, it registers three media types and defines a file format for storage uses such as email.
sections.eli5: It is a rulebook for putting a certain kind of squeezed-down voice into internet packages and into saved files.

sections.title: The EVRC-NW Codec and Its Frames
sections.content:
EVRC-NW extends both EVRC-B and EVRC-WB, which were developed in 3GPP2, and adds DTX support. It works on 20 ms frames. The default sampling rate is 16 kHz (wideband), and 8 kHz (narrowband) input and output is also supported.

The codec has eight modes, 0 to 7, defined in 3GPP2 C.S0014-D. Modes 0, 1 and 7 are interoperable with EVRC-WB, and modes 1 to 7 are interoperable with EVRC-B. By default EVRC-NW supports all narrowband modes (1 to 7); support for wideband mode (mode 0) is optional.

Each frame comes out in one of four sizes: 171 bits (full rate), 80 bits (1/2 rate), 40 bits (1/4 rate) or 16 bits (1/8 rate). There are also two zero-bit frame types, blank and erasure. A sender SHOULD NOT transmit erasure frames. The most important service the RFC names is IP telephony.
sections.eli5: The codec chops speech into tiny 20 millisecond slices and squeezes each slice into one of a few sizes, like choosing a small, medium or large envelope depending on how much is going on in the sound.

sections.title: RTP Header Usage
sections.content:
The RTP header is used as in RFC 3550. Even if the encoder input or decoder output runs at 8 kHz, a 16 kHz RTP clock rate MUST always be used. The decoder does not need to know the sampling rate used at the encoder.

The RTP timestamp goes up by 320 for each 20 milliseconds. The marker bit (M) is set to 1 if the first frame in the packet is the first speech frame of a talkspurt, and to 0 for all other packets.
sections.eli5: Every packet carries a clock tick count. Here the clock always ticks the wideband way, and the marker bit says "someone just started talking".

sections.title: Payload Formats and the Capability Flag
sections.content:
Three packet formats are supported: interleaved/bundled, header-free and compact bundled. Their TOC, interleaving, DTX and bundling behavior is the same as in the earlier EVRC RFCs (RFC 3558, RFC 4788 and RFC 5188), with three changes to the interleaved/bundled format.

  • The mode change request field MUST be read according to the RATE_REDUC parameter for EVRC-NW in 3GPP2 C.S0014-D.
  • An EVRC-NW encoder in a one-to-one session SHOULD honor the mode change request.
  • The reserved field in the first octet has only one bit. Bit 1 is a new encoding capability flag (C).

C=0 means the local encoder can do mode 0 wideband encoding. C=1 means it can only do narrowband encoding. The far end uses this to decide what to ask for with the MMM mode request field. For example, if a called endpoint loses wideband ability mid-call, it sets C=1 and the caller can switch its request from mode 0 to mode 4 for bandwidth efficiency or to mode 1 for best perceived quality.

The media type audio/EVRCNW maps to the interleaved/bundled format, audio/EVRCNW0 to the header-free format and audio/EVRCNW1 to the compact bundled format.
sections.eli5: There is a tiny flag in each packet that says "I can send you hi-fi voice" or "I can only do ordinary voice", so the listener knows what it is allowed to ask for.

sections.title: The Storage File Format
sections.content:
For files or email attachments, the file starts with a magic number that identifies the codec: the ASCII string #!EVRCNW\n, bytes 0x23 0x21 0x45 0x56 0x52 0x43 0x4E 0x57 0x0A. The registration lists the file extensions enw and ENW.

Codec frames follow in order. Each is prefixed by a single TOC octet, made by setting the four most significant bits to zero, so a full-rate frame (value 4) is stored as 0x04. Frames lost in transmission and frames never received MUST be stored as erasure frames (TOC value 5) so the file stays in step with the original audio.
sections.eli5: When saving to a file, every little voice piece gets a label saying how big it is. If a piece went missing, a blank placeholder is saved so the timing stays right.

sections.title: Media Types and SDP Negotiation
sections.content:
Section 9 registers the three audio subtypes. Optional parameters include mode-set-recv, ptime, maxptime (not for EVRCNW0), maxinterleave (EVRCNW only), fixedrate (EVRCNW1 only) and the DTX parameters silencesupp, dtxmax, dtxmin and hangover. If maxinterleave is not signaled, it MUST be 5.

In SDP, the subtype goes into a=rtpmap, ptime and maxptime go in their own attributes, and the remaining parameters go in a=fmtp. With the offer/answer model of RFC 3264, an offerer SHOULD also list EVRC-B and EVRC-WB, with EVRC-NW preferred, so that an answerer that only knows the older codecs can still pick one.

mode-set-recv is a receive-only preference: a decoder tells the sender which modes it prefers. When it is absent, the set is modes 1 to 7. A sender may ignore it, but must not assume the other side supports mode 0 unless the offer lists it or MMM=0 requests arrive. For EVRCNW1, the whole session MUST use one fixed rate and mode. The old sendmode attribute is deprecated in EVRC-NW.
sections.eli5: Before a call, each side lists the voice types it understands, favorite first. The other side picks one both know, like agreeing on a language before chatting.

sections.title: Mode Change Requests
sections.content:
The 3-bit MMM field lets a node tell the far end which compression mode it prefers. The idea, called the Capacity Operating Point, is a trade-off between voice quality and network capacity. When the network is lightly loaded, vocoders can run at higher average bit rates for better quality. When load rises, lower-rate modes help avoid a sharp rise in frame erasures.

In mobile-to-mobile calls both ends have their own network load, so a node that prefers a higher rate should still adjust to a lower rate if the far end asks. If a requested mode is not supported, the RFC recommends using the next lower average bit-rate mode that is supported.

A wideband-capable endpoint can look at the C bit. If it is 1, the far end cannot send mode 0, so the request can depend only on local load. If it is 0, mode 0 can be requested knowing it will be supported.
sections.eli5: If the road is jammed, you ask your friend to talk in a shorter, simpler way so everything fits. If the road is clear, you ask for the best quality.

sections.title: Congestion and Security
sections.content:
Congestion control is left to RFC 3550 and applicable RTP profiles such as RFC 3551. The RFC notes that packing more frames into each RTP packet reduces the number of packets and header overhead, but increases delay and reduces error robustness.

For security, the RFC says compression is applied end-to-end and the encodings do not show significant non-uniformity. Implementations are subject to the security considerations of RFC 3558, RFC 3550 and any appropriate profile. It points to RFC 6562 for additional considerations.
sections.eli5: Putting more voice slices in one package saves packaging but means waiting longer and losing more if one package gets lost.
